title: Comparing Decimals Worksheets Through Hundredths
intro: Compare matching place values, starting with the whole-number part. More decimal digits do not always mean a greater number.
html:
Use the same-sized whole

When decimals describe amounts, compare amounts measured with the same unit or based on equal-sized wholes. Half of a large sheet and half of a small sheet are not equal areas just because both fractions are one half.

Line up the decimal points

Compare whole-number parts first. If they match, compare tenths, then hundredths. The first different place decides which number is greater. For 2.34 and 2.39, the ones and tenths match. Four hundredths is less than nine hundredths, so 2.34 < 2.39.

More digits do not mean more value

Think of 0.8 as 0.80. Eighty hundredths is greater than seventy-five hundredths, so 0.8 > 0.75. Compare matching places instead of treating 8 and 75 as whole-number parts.

If the columns are confusing: write ones, tenths, and hundredths above the numbers. Put each digit under its place. Start on the left and stop at the first different digit.

Trailing zeros keep the value

0.5 = 0.50 because five tenths equals fifty hundredths. A zero at the end of the decimal part does not change its value. A zero between the decimal point and another digit matters: 0.05 is five hundredths, not five tenths.

Read and explain the symbol

The open side of > or < faces the greater value. Read your comparison aloud. An explanation should name the first different place, or explain why every matching place is equal. Use the space to align digits or write a short reason.

What this practice includes

Each set selects six distinct original pairs: four symbol questions and two questions that explicitly ask for a place-value explanation. Values range from 0 through 9.99, with at most two decimal places. Whole numbers may appear, and trailing zeros are omitted. An equal pair is possible but is not guaranteed in each set.

The answer key gives the original comparison symbols. An adult should check explanations separately. This supports selected hundredths-comparison practice; it does not provide visual models or assess every part of the standard.
